stoic

STOH-ik -- two syllables, stress on STOH. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Stoic is not showing feeling or emotion.

The captain remained stoic as the storm shredded the sails, giving orders in the same calm, level voice.

Example

In the dentist's chair, the girl has a tooth pulled and simply sits still, hands folded, her face never changing.

Enduring pain or difficulty without letting any emotion show is what stoic describes. A stoic person may feel plenty inside -- the point is that nothing reaches their face or voice.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

unemotional: Unemotional means not displaying feelings, and it often hints the feelings barely exist -- an unemotional report reads as bare fact. Stoic is warmer underneath: a stoic person may feel a great deal and simply refuses to let pain or fear show while they endure it.

uncomplaining: Uncomplaining means bearing hardship without protesting -- an uncomplaining patient never grumbles about the pain. It is only about what you say. Stoic goes further: a stoic person lets nothing show, keeping pain out of their face and voice, not just their words.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

emotional: showing feelings openly and strongly

demonstrative: expressing feelings openly, especially affection

Where it sits · how completely feeling stays hidden — composed → stoic → impassive

composed vs. stoic: Composed is milder than stoic -- a composed person stays calm and collected but may still let a flicker of feeling show, while a stoic person reveals nothing at all, even under real pain or pressure.

impassive vs. stoic: Impassive is, if anything, even blanker than stoic: stoic suggests feelings deliberately endured and mastered, while impassive describes a face so unreadable you cannot tell whether anything is felt at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — stoa

root — stoa: porch, colonnade (Greek stoa)

suffix — -ic

suffix — -ic: having the characteristics of; like (Greek -ikos, via Latin -icus)

Put it together

Put it together: Stoic traces to Greek stoa, 'porch.' In ancient Athens, a group of philosophers taught beneath a famous painted porch -- the Stoa Poikile -- and were nicknamed for it. Because they prized calm self-control above all, 'stoic' came to describe anyone who endures hardship without showing emotion. The everyday word you are learning here is that lowercase adjective.

Use the root in a new word: stoically

Use the root in a new word: stoically: She stoically endured the three-hour delay without a single word of complaint.

In everyday use -- and on the ISEE -- stoic means not showing feeling or emotion: a stoic expression, a stoic silence, stoic endurance. With a capital S, Stoic names the ancient Greek school of philosophy the word came from; that is history, not the sense being tested.
